messages.content:
Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-polish-long-0050", "row_sha256": "8078c35adfd236f9b3bc160d8a26d26a92bf97f6dea3d3ad65255bc4f42ece5d", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
at north quay cooperative, the payroll export is prepared every other tuesday for the two-week pay period. this one covered may 4 through may 17, and the file was due in the accounting system by 2 p.m. on may 19. the export has 86 employee rows and comes from the payroll staging workbook, which takes approved hours from harborclock. the workbook also carries overtime hours, employee numbers, department names, and cost center codes. the accounting system is called ledgerway, and it accepts a comma-separated file with a fixed set of columns. lena ortiz, the payroll coordinator, assembled the file at 10:15 that morning. dev shah, the systems analyst, checked the export layout and the transfer records. the file was still marked as a draft while they reviewed it, and the approved pay amounts were not being changed during this review.

the problem showed up in the cost center column, not in the hours or pay columns. seven employees had moved temporarily between departments during the pay period, and their harborclock records carried a temporary transfer code. the payroll staging workbook had the employee numbers and hours for those rows, but it did not fill in a cost center for the transfer code. the affected employees were assigned across three departments, and the blank fields appeared in rows 12, 19, 33, 46, 61, 70, and 82. the regular department column still showed each employee's home department. it did not tell the reviewers which cost center should receive the temporary hours, so they did not use that column as a replacement.

lena opened the transfer log beside the workbook and compared the dates with the time records. the log showed that four of the seven transfers began partway through the pay period, while three covered the full period. two entries had a return date entered, and the other five had no return date recorded. the missing return dates did not mean the employees had stayed in the temporary departments after may 17; the log simply did not provide a later date. dev checked whether the transfer code had been used consistently in harborclock and found it was present on all seven affected rows. he did not infer a cost center from the code itself because the code named a type of transfer, not a department or account.

lena said, “we can correct the mapping table once the department owners confirm the temporary assignments, but do not charge accounts from these blank fields.” that was the instruction attached to the draft review. the restriction applied to account charging based on those seven unresolved cost center fields. it did not stop the team from correcting the mapping table, checking employee numbers, or preparing the rest of the export for review. no one was asked to change the approved hours or to select a cost center solely to make the file complete. the seven rows remained identifiable by employee number and pay-period dates while the source records were checked.

1. compare the employee number and transfer dates in harborclock with the entries in the transfer log. 2. ask the relevant department owners to confirm the temporary assignments and the cost center for the hours in question. 3. update the mapping table only after the confirmation is received, then regenerate the draft and check that the seven rows carry the confirmed codes. the steps were written in the review notes because the transfer log and workbook were maintained by different teams. the notes also say to keep the original draft in the payroll review folder, rather than replacing it while questions about the assignments remain open.

the review folder already contained the may 4 to may 17 draft, the transfer log downloaded that morning, and a copy of the harborclock detail report. the draft file was named nq_payroll_0504-0517_draft.csv, and the detail report included the employee number, date, hours, and transfer code. dev checked the column order against the ledgerway import guide: employee number, regular hours, overtime hours, gross pay, department, and cost center. the file had all six columns in that order. the seven cost center cells were blank, while the gross pay and hour totals matched the staging workbook. those checks were recorded separately from the unresolved assignment question.

at 11:05, lena sent a message to the three department owners whose teams had employees in the affected rows. she included the seven employee numbers and the transfer dates, but not pay amounts, because the question was about assignment codes. she asked each owner to confirm which cost center applied to the temporary hours and to point out any date that did not match their records. she did not ask them to approve payroll or to revise employee hours. the message noted that the file remained a draft and that the cost center fields would stay blank until the assignment information was confirmed. the three owners had different schedules, so the replies were expected through the usual shared mailbox rather than in one meeting.

while waiting for those replies, dev reviewed the other 79 rows for the same transfer code and found none. he also checked that the export did not contain duplicate employee numbers and that each row had a department value. one employee had overtime hours and another had no overtime, but both entries matched the staging workbook; neither was among the seven blank cost center rows. lena wrote down these checks in the existing review sheet, with the time of each check and the file name used. she kept the review sheet separate from the transfer log so that checking the file would not alter the underlying records.

the team could still make routine corrections that did not resolve the disputed assignment, such as fixing a misspelled department label if it differed from the approved roster. no department label needed correction in this draft. if an owner identified a date discrepancy, lena would compare it with the harborclock detail before changing the transfer record; she would not treat a reply alone as a change to recorded hours. if an owner confirmed the cost center but the dates remained unclear, the row would remain out of the mapping update until the date question was addressed. these conditions were written beside the steps so a partial reply would not be treated as confirmation of every field.

the current review sheet lists the file name, the may 4 to may 17 period, the seven affected row numbers, and the names of the three department owners contacted. it records that the regular department values are present and that the seven cost center values are blank. it also notes the time the transfer log and harborclock detail were checked, and that the file was still a draft when the checks were entered. the shared mailbox was where the owners' replies would be kept, while the review folder remained the place for the draft, source report, transfer log, and review sheet.", "output": "North Quay Cooperative prepares its payroll export every other Tuesday for the two-week pay period. This export covered May 4 through May 17, and the file was due in the accounting system by 2 p.m. on May 19. It contains 86 employee rows and comes from the payroll staging workbook, which takes approved hours from HarborClock. The workbook also carries overtime hours, employee numbers, department names, and cost center codes. The accounting system is called Ledgerway, and it accepts a comma-separated file with a fixed set of columns. Lena Ortiz, the payroll coordinator, assembled the file at 10:15 that morning. Dev Shah, the systems analyst, checked the export layout and transfer records. The file was still marked as a draft during their review, and they were not changing the approved pay amounts.

The problem appeared in the cost center column, not in the hours or pay columns. Seven employees had moved temporarily between departments during the pay period, and their HarborClock records carried a temporary transfer code. The payroll staging workbook had employee numbers and hours for those rows, but it did not fill in a cost center for the transfer code. The affected employees were assigned across three departments, and the blank fields appeared in rows 12, 19, 33, 46, 61, 70, and 82. The regular department column still showed each employee’s home department. It did not indicate which cost center should receive the temporary hours, so the reviewers did not use it as a substitute.

Lena opened the transfer log beside the workbook and compared its dates with the time records. The log showed that four of the seven transfers began partway through the pay period, while three covered the full period. Two entries had a return date, and the other five had no return date recorded. The missing return dates did not mean that the employees had stayed in the temporary departments after May 17; the log simply did not provide a later date. Dev checked whether the transfer code had been used consistently in HarborClock and found it on all seven affected rows. He did not infer a cost center from the code itself because it named a type of transfer, not a department or account.

Lena said, “We can correct the mapping table once the department owners confirm the temporary assignments, but do not charge accounts from these blank fields.” That was the instruction attached to the draft review. The restriction applied to account charging based on those seven unresolved cost center fields. It did not prevent the team from correcting the mapping table, checking employee numbers, or preparing the rest of the export for review. No one was asked to change the approved hours or select a cost center solely to make the file complete. The seven rows remained identifiable by employee number and pay-period dates while the source records were checked.

1. Compare the employee number and transfer dates in HarborClock with the entries in the transfer log. 2. Ask the relevant department owners to confirm the temporary assignments and the cost center for the hours in question. 3. Update the mapping table only after receiving confirmation, then regenerate the draft and check that the seven rows carry the confirmed codes. The steps were written in the review notes because the transfer log and workbook were maintained by different teams. The notes also say to keep the original draft in the payroll review folder rather than replacing it while questions about the assignments remain open.

The review folder already contained the May 4 to May 17 draft, the transfer log downloaded that morning, and a copy of the HarborClock detail report. The draft file was named nq_payroll_0504-0517_draft.csv, and the detail report included the employee number, date, hours, and transfer code. Dev checked the column order against the Ledgerway import guide: employee number, regular hours, overtime hours, gross pay, department, and cost center. The file had all six columns in that order. The seven cost center cells were blank, while the gross pay and hour totals matched the staging workbook. Those checks were recorded separately from the unresolved assignment question.

At 11:05, Lena sent a message to the three department owners whose teams had employees in the affected rows. She included the seven employee numbers and transfer dates, but not pay amounts, because the question concerned assignment codes. She asked each owner to confirm which cost center applied to the temporary hours and to point out any dates that did not match their records. She did not ask them to approve payroll or revise employee hours. The message noted that the file remained a draft and that the cost center fields would stay blank until the assignment information was confirmed. The three owners had different schedules, so replies were expected through the usual shared mailbox rather than in one meeting.

While waiting for the replies, Dev reviewed the other 79 rows for the same transfer code and found none. He also checked that the export did not contain duplicate employee numbers and that each row had a department value. One employee had overtime hours and another had none, but both entries matched the staging workbook; neither was among the seven rows with blank cost centers. Lena recorded these checks in the existing review sheet, along with the time of each check and the file name used. She kept the review sheet separate from the transfer log so that checking the file would not alter the underlying records.

The team could still make routine corrections that did not resolve the disputed assignment, such as fixing a misspelled department label if it differed from the approved roster. No department label needed correction in this draft. If an owner identified a date discrepancy, Lena would compare it with the HarborClock detail before changing the transfer record; she would not treat a reply alone as a change to recorded hours. If an owner confirmed the cost center but the dates remained unclear, the row would remain out of the mapping update until the date question was addressed. These conditions were written beside the steps so that a partial reply would not be treated as confirmation of every field.

The current review sheet lists the file name, the May 4 to May 17 period, the seven affected row numbers, and the names of the three department owners contacted. It records that the regular department values are present and that the seven cost center values are blank. It also notes when the transfer log and HarborClock detail were checked, and that the file was still a draft when the checks were entered. The shared mailbox was where the owners’ replies would be kept, while the review folder remained the place for the draft, source report, transfer log, and review sheet."}]
